papers.title: Symptoms of anxiety are linked to N3 sleep and lower dissipation of slow-wave activity during nocturnal sleep.
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) is vital for brain health, memory, and emotional resilience. Slow-wave activity (SWA) reflects homeostatic sleep pressure, which dissipates across successive sleep cycles. Impaired SWA dissipation has been linked to depression. We examined whether reduced SWA dissipation is associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression in healthy conscripts. Seventy conscripts (67 males, aged 18-24) undergoing compulsory military service participated in overnight polysomnography. SWA dissipation was assessed by comparing normalized delta (0.5-4.0 Hz) electroencephalogram power between first and third NREM sleep episodes. This was complemented by full spectral analysis of sleep stages. Psychological measures included Overall Anxiety Severity and Impairment Scale, Beck's Depression Inventory, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Conscripts with elevated anxiety (24%) exhibited weaker SWA dissipation and greater proportion of N3 sleep. Similarly, anxiety was negatively correlated with SWA dissipation and positively with proportion of N3. Additionally, conscripts with elevated anxiety but without elevated depressiveness had less REM sleep than those with both anxiety and depression, as well as those without symptoms. Findings related to sleepiness or depression without anxiety were limited. In full spectral analysis individuals with higher anxiety exhibited elevated alpha power during REM sleep, potentially reflecting cortical hyperarousal. Higher proportion of N3 sleep and lower SWA dissipation were associated with greater anxiety rather than depression. These findings highlight the importance of adequate SWS in emotion regulation. Impaired SWA dissipation may contribute to preservation of negative emotional memories during sleep. Another possibility is that hyperarousal increases need for recovery sleep.

papers.title: Irreversible functional network deformation induced by preprocessing scheme order in multivariate EEG recordings.
papers.abstract: The analysis of Electroencephalographic recordings is non-trivial, the order in which filtering and re-referencing are applied during multivariate signal preprocessing has a critical and underappreciated consequence for functional network estimation. Using EEG sleep recordings from healthy subjects, synthetic data from controlled numerical models (Nf-Tori and IAAFT surrogates), and surrogate-based statistical testing, we provide a quantitative comparison of two preprocessing schemes that differ solely in the order of filtering and re-referencing (filtering followed by re-referencing-FR, and re-referencing followed by filtering-RF). We show that the RF scheme induces spurious cross-correlations that increase systematically with the frequency band and are strongly modulated by the power spectral exponent β of the signal. Critically, for signals with steep power spectra (β ≥2), a regime that characterizes slow-wave sleep, epileptic post-ictal periods, anesthesia, neonatal, and patients in vegetative states, the RF scheme produces artificial correlations that are irreversible. They cannot be eliminated post-hoc even when surrogate-corrected cross-correlations (SAC-matrix) are applied. The mechanism underlying this effect is due to the high-amplitude slow-frequency components that dominate the median reference signal over extended time intervals, embedding redundant information across all channels. In contrast, the FR scheme introduces only small, systematic negative shifts in cross-correlations that are not statistically significant and can be effectively corrected using surrogate-based methods. We therefore recommend the FR scheme combined with surrogate-corrected cross-correlations for all applications involving signals with β ≥2. Although this finding is demonstrated in EEG, it applies to any multivariate recording where spatial re-referencing and band-pass filtering are applied sequentially.

papers.title: Inhibition of Cerebellar Dentate Nucleus-Zona Incerta Glutamatergic Circuit Improves Sleep Disturbances in Chronic Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Model.
papers.abstract: Patients with chronic temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) frequently experience various sleep disorders, characterized by reduced sleep duration, diminished sleep stages, and disrupted sleep patterns. Recent research has identified a population of GABAergic neurons in the ventral zona incerta (ZI) that is instrumental in promoting sleep, along with a neural pathway that connects the cerebellar dentate nucleus (CDN) to the ZI. However, the precise role of this circuit in regulating sleep patterns remains inadequately understood. This study employed anatomical, chemogenetic, optogenetic, and immunofluorescence staining techniques to investigate the potential of the CDN-ZI circuit in ameliorating sleep disturbances associated with TLE. Our findings indicate that pilocarpine-treated mice exhibit significant sleep fragmentation and reduced sleep duration, particularly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. By employing optogenetic and chemogenetic methods to target CDN glutamatergic neurons, we observed a decrease in sleep fragmentation, an increase in overall sleep duration, and an enhancement in sleep quality in pilocarpine-treated mice. The inhibition of the CDN-ZI glutamatergic circuit through optogenetic and chemogenetic methods resulted in substantial improvements in sleep disturbances following TLE. Targeting the CDN-ZI glutamatergic circuit represents a promising therapeutic strategy for addressing sleep disorders resulting from chronic TLE.

papers.title: Enhanced local synchronization with impaired large-scale recruitment of NREM slow waves in pediatric disorders of arousal
papers.abstract: NREM slow waves emerge from the synchronization of neuronal activity across multiple spatial scales. During childhood, local synchronization and large-scale propagation undergo distinct maturational trajectories, paralleling cortical synaptic remodeling and the maturation of long-range brain connectivity. How alterations in this local-to-global organization relate to arousal instability remains poorly understood. Here, we used 256-channel high-density EEG to characterize NREM oscillatory organization in 17 children with disorders of arousal (DOA) and 17 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Children with DOA showed a marked dissociation between local synchronization and large-scale coordination: slow waves were locally larger, steeper and more synchronized, yet recruited the cortex less globally and exhibited a more spatially restricted distribution of origins. This phenotype preferentially involved Type 1 slow waves, a subtype associated with widespread cortical and subcortico-cortical recruitment and late developmental maturation. Children with DOA also showed reduced centro-posterior slow spindle density, providing convergent evidence for altered coordination of distributed NREM oscillations. These microstructural abnormalities occurred despite largely preserved conventional sleep architecture. Together, our findings reveal an altered local-to-global organization of NREM sleep in pediatric DOA and suggest that vulnerability to incomplete arousals may emerge when strong local synchronization is not matched by effective large-scale network coordination during brain development.

papers.title: Sleep-dependent modulation of thalamic brain temperature estimates in humans
papers.abstract: Mammalian thermal physiology is geared towards dissipating heat during sleep. Brain temperature typically decreases during non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep in all mammalian species measured to date, yet non-invasive confirmation in healthy humans is lacking: the only available human study used invasive recordings in epileptic patients without a wake control condition. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables brain temperature mapping non-invasively, using the temperature-sensitive chemical shift of water relative to N-Acetyl-Aspartate as an internal reference. First, we validated that with metabolite cycling (MC), a MRS approach that enables the simultaneous acquisition of metabolite and water information without conventional water suppression, can be used to determine estimates of brain temperature in an ex vivo sheep head. Next, we determined that by using a temporal resolution of ~4 minutes, we obtained high-quality spectra without losing excessive temporal resolution. We then re-analyzed an existing set of MRS data (acquired with the MC sequence) of the thalamus in young adults (n=9) who slept in the evening for up to 2 hours in the scanner, to assess sleep-evoked changes in estimates of brain temperature. Of the nine participants, five participants took part in the subsequent wake-only experiment, allowing to control for the potential impact of circadian time and body posture on estimates of brain temperature. Sleep-wake states were quantified with standard polysomnography, confirming that the participants managed to sleep in the scanner. On average, they spent 39.4+/-15.7 min in N2 sleep, 24.8+/-18.1 min in N3 sleep, 10.0+/-4.9 min in N1 sleep, and 37.0+/-19.6 min awake. Estimates of brain temperature were correlated across the sleep and wake-only experiment within the same participant (R^2=0.29, P<0.0001). When participants entered NREM sleep, estimates of brain temperature decreased by 0.2 degrees Celcius. Moreover, the deeper NREM sleep, the more pronounced the decrease in estimates of brain temperature (P=0.014). These data suggest that an evening nap consisting of NREM sleep decreases thalamic temperature. Considering the profound impact temperature can have on brain functioning, these brain temperature changes could be a pathway through which sleep impacts the brain.

papers.title: Pharmacological Inhibition of Histamine N-Methyltransferase Markedly Improves Hypersomnia in a Mouse Model of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. In addition to motor symptoms, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) occurs frequently in patients with PD and severely impairs their quality of life. Current pharmacotherapies for EDS in PD are often associated with adverse effects. However, clinical studies have yielded inconsistent results, underscoring the need for safer, more effective treatment strategies. Histamine plays a pivotal role in maintaining wakefulness in the brain and is primarily inactivated by histamine N-methyltransferase (HNMT), the major enzyme responsible for histamine clearance in the central nervous system. We previously demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of HNMT markedly elevates brain histamine levels and potently promotes wakefulness in mouse models of narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia, suggesting that targeting HNMT may also be beneficial for treating hypersomnia in PD. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of HNMT ameliorates hypersomnia in a 6-hydroxydopamine-induced mouse model of PD. We first confirmed dopaminergic neuronal loss and hypersomnia during the active phase in a mouse model of PD. Pharmacological inhibition of HNMT with metoprine robustly increased wakefulness, markedly reduced NREM and REM sleep, and prolonged sleep latency. Metoprine also reduced sleep-wake bout fragmentation, indicating the sustained consolidation of wakefulness. In direct comparison, metoprine produced stronger and more sustained wake-promoting effects than other wake-promoting agents. These findings indicate that HNMT inhibition represents a promising and mechanistically distinct therapeutic approach for EDS in PD.

papers.title: Hyperglycaemia reversibly disrupts circadian behaviour in mice
papers.abstract: Disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms are among the most common features of diabetes, and are known to raise the risk of developing the disease. Whether the relationship also runs the other way, with diabetes itself disrupting the clock, has remained unresolved. Using an inducible mouse model of diabetes, in which hyperglycaemia can be induced and then reversed within the same animal, we show that elevated blood glucose is a reversible cause of circadian disruption. Raising blood glucose reduced the amplitude of circadian rest-activity rhythms by 50%, in proportion to the degree of hyperglycaemia, and shortened the free-running period of the clock. Restoring normoglycaemia reversed both effects. Diabetic animals had a delayed phase of activity onset, i.e. later chronotype, and re-entrained more slowly after a simulated jet lag. However, phase shifting to nocturnal light pulses was intact, suggesting normal photic responses. Brain glucose and O-GlcNAcylation, a nutrient-sensitive protein modification, were both elevated in diabetic animals, showing that peripheral hyperglycaemia reaches the brain and alters its metabolic state, and providing a molecular readout of that exposure. Together, these findings establish that a peripheral metabolic state is a reversible determinant of circadian rest-activity behaviour, completing a bidirectional link between blood glucose and the clock and arguing that the two must be treated together rather than in isolation.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation impairs ventral hippocampus-medial prefrontal connectivity and task learning in rats.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for memory consolidation, and sleep loss has long been associated with cognitive impairment. However, the circuit-level mechanisms through which sleep deprivation disrupts hippocampal-prefrontal communication during learning remain poorly understood. Here, we combined a T-maze learning task with simultaneous local field potential (LFP) recordings in the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of rats. Using dynamic causal modeling (DCM), we quantified directional connectivity during task acquisition under normal and sleep-deprived conditions. We found that learning strengthened forward connectivity from vHPC to mPFC while weakening backward connectivity from mPFC to vHPC. Sleep deprivation impaired this forward connectivity, resulting in slower learning and reduced task accuracy. These findings characterize the altered circuit dynamics by which sleep loss disrupts hippocampal-prefrontal circuit dynamics, providing insight into how impaired cross-regional communication may underlie cognitive deficits observed in sleep-related psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: White noise as a non-pharmacological intervention for enhancing the recovery of rats with wound-associated sleep disorders.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are one of the common symptoms in patients with wounds, which can hinder recovery. Commonly used hypnotic medications in clinical practice are short-acting but carry risks of adverse reactions and drug abuse. As a non-invasive acoustic intervention, white noise can regulate brain electroencephalographic rhythms to improve sleep disorders. However, the interventional effects and rehabilitation outcomes of white noise on wounds with sleep disorders remain unclear. A wound model with sleep disorders was established in rats by integrating para-chlorophenylalanine-induced sleep deprivation with full-thickness skin excision. The rats were randomly allocated into three groups: white noise (WN), alprazolam (ALP), and control (Model). Sleep status was evaluated using pentobarbital supra-threshold dose synergistic sleep tests, circadian activity monitoring, and serum 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) level measurements. Inflammatory responses were assessed via blood routine examinations and serological analyses. Histological and immunohistochemical evaluations were performed to examine the structural features of the wounds. Compared with the control group, the WN group showed significantly reduced sleep latency and inflammatory markers, as well as increased sleep duration, body weight gain rate, and wound healing rate. After prolonged intervention, the newly formed tissue in the WN group exhibited a lower epidermal-dermal ratio, collagen fibers that were orderly and loosely arranged, decreased neovascularization, and thus more closely resembled the morphology of normal skin compared to the Model group. WN promotes the long-term restoration of sleep and body weight in rats with wound-induced sleep disturbances. WN regulates inflammatory responses, facilitating inflammation resolution and expediting the transition to the repair phase.

papers.title: Circadian timing does not modulate human temporal contrast sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have reported diurnal variations in color perception and luminance contrast sensitivity, suggesting modulation of visual processing by the circadian pacemaker. To clarify potential time-of-day effects, we examined whether cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity is modulated by circadian timing. We disentangled circadian and homeostatic influences on human visual performance using a 40-hour forced desynchrony protocol. Twelve participants (five female participants, 24.4 ± 2.9 years, range 19-30) followed a repeating 3.75-hour cycle comprising 2 hours 30 minutes of wakefulness and 1 hour 15 minutes of sleep under constant environmental conditions. Circadian period was estimated from up to 46 salivary melatonin samples per participant. During wake periods, participants repeatedly completed temporal contrast sensitivity tasks at 2 Hz and 8 Hz, using tasks that probed both luminance (L+M+S) and chromatic (L-M, S-cone-directed) modulations. We tested for circadian modulation of visual performance by comparing hierarchical cosinor models with intercept-only null models using Bayes factors. All participants showed robust melatonin rhythms (mean τ = 24.18 ± 0.39 hours). Bayesian inference provided decisive evidence against circadian variation in luminance or chromatic contrast sensitivity. Within this controlled protocol, we found no detectable near-24-hour modulation of cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity. Previously reported time-of-day effects may instead reflect homeostatic influences, pupil-linked changes in retinal illuminance, or mechanisms outside the cone-mediated pathways probed here. By separating circadian phase from sleep-wake-related influences, this study clarifies when circadian modulation of visual performance can and cannot be inferred.

papers.title: Investigating the transfer of physical stimuli to the dreamed body: A comparative study of muscular, vestibular, and haptic stimulation on dream incorporation.
papers.abstract: The relationship between the dreamed body and the physical body remains an open question in sleep and dream research. This study examined whether somatosensory stimulation applied during REM sleep modulates the corresponding dream content under controlled conditions. Using a within-subject design, we compared three stimulation modalities-electrical muscular, galvanic vestibular, and haptic vibration-each paired with a modality-specific sham stimulation. Twenty-four participants completed one adaptation night followed by three consecutive experimental nights in the sleep laboratory. Dream reports were collected following rapid eye movement sleep awakenings after stimulation or sham periods, yielding a total of 120 reports. Dream incorporation of bodily sensations and actions was observed across all conditions; however, generalized linear mixed-effects analyses revealed no statistically significant differences between stimulation and sham conditions for any modality. No evidence for reliable modality-specific dream incorporation was observed under rigorous sham-controlled conditions. Rather than demonstrating robust stimulation-specific effects, these findings suggest that contextual and expectancy-related influences substantially contribute to bodily dream content under laboratory conditions while highlighting methodological challenges in dream incorporation research. By combining multiple somatosensory stimulation modalities with rigorous sham-controlled procedures, the present study provides a methodological benchmark for future investigations of dream incorporation and dream engineering.

papers.title: Human-artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time.
papers.abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions.

papers.title: Loss of hepatic circadian organization in fatty liver syndrome identifies CLOCK as a regulator of lipid homeostasis in laying hens.
papers.abstract: Fatty liver syndrome (FLS) is a major metabolic disorder in laying hens, but how hepatic lipid dysregulation is linked to circadian disruption remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of circadian regulation in FLS pathogenesis and focused on the core clock gene Clock Circadian Regulator (CLOCK). In a high-fat diet-induced FLS model in Lohmann pink layers, affected birds showed hepatomegaly, hepatic lipid accumulation, elevated serum total cholesterol, triglycerides, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase, increased hepatic pro-inflammatory gene expression, and reduced interleukin-10 (IL-10) expression. FLS was also accompanied by reduced laying performance, delayed and dispersed oviposition, and altered temporal profiles of reproductive hormones. Time-series liver transcriptomics across six circadian time points showed extensive transcriptional remodeling in FLS, with dysregulated genes enriched mainly in lipid metabolic and circadian pathways. Pathway analyses indicated increased fatty acid biosynthesis together with reduced fatty acid degradation, glycerophospholipid metabolism, and ether lipid metabolism. Rhythmicity analysis further revealed a marked collapse of hepatic circadian organization: the number of rhythmically expressed genes decreased from 1,046 in controls to 81 in FLS, and core clock genes including CLOCK, cryptochrome 2 (CRY2), and basic helix-loop-helix family member e40 (BHLHE40) lost rhythmic expression. Series Test of Cluster analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and protein-protein interaction analysis consistently placed CLOCK at the center of the circadian regulatory network associated with hepatic metabolic disturbance. Functional assays in primary chicken hepatocytes showed that CLOCK overexpression reduced lipid accumulation, intracellular total cholesterol and triglyceride levels, and expression of lipogenic genes, while increasing peroxisome proliferation-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) expression and altering multiple circadian regulators. In an oleic acid-induced steatosis model, CLOCK overexpression similarly reduced lipid deposition and inflammatory gene expression, while increasing IL-10, nicotinamide phosphoribosyl transferase (NAMPT), and Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) expression. This study provides mechanistic insight into the circadian basis of FLS and highlights CLOCK as a potential molecular target for the prevention and intervention of metabolic liver disorders in poultry.

papers.title: Lighting and circadian cues shape locomotor strategies for balance and navigation in larval zebrafish.
papers.abstract: Most fish are inherently unstable and must swim to stabilize posture. How diurnal fish reduce activity at night while maintaining postural control remains unclear. We defined distinct locomotor strategies that larval zebrafish (Danio rerio) use to control posture and navigate the water column in response to light and circadian cues. In the dark, larvae maintain balance by swimming in long bouts with large nose-up rotations, compensating for nose-down drift accrued during prolonged inactivity. Effective postural compensation requires vestibular sensation from the utricle. By contrast, in the light, larvae navigate with short, frequent and variable bouts. While lighting exerts a dominant, masking effect on the locomotor strategies, circadian rhythms modulate swim kinematics. Our results reveal distinct light-dark locomotor strategies and disentangle how ambient light and the internal clock jointly shape balance control and navigation. This work lays the foundation for understanding how external and internal cues interact to govern locomotor activity in freely moving diurnal animals.

papers.title: Associations Between Resting-State EEG Delta-band Activity at Selected Parietal Electrodes and Cognitive Changes Following Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment: An Exploratory Analysis.
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation (taVNS) may improve cognition in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), but its electrophysiological correlates remain unclear. We explored whether parietal delta-band changes were associated with cognitive changes following taVNS. This exploratory secondary analysis included 26 participants with MCI from a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (taVNS, n = 14; sham, n = 12) who had valid resting-state EEG data at baseline and Week 24. Absolute and relative 1-3 Hz delta power at Pz, P1, P2, and P5 were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA and EEG-cognitive correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Absolute delta power showed significant time effects at all four electrodes after FDR correction (all q = 0.008). Relative delta power at Pz showed an uncorrected group effect (F = 5.007, p = 0.035; q = 0.218). In the taVNS group, MoCA-B improvement was positively associated with relative delta-power changes at P1, P2, and P5 (r = 0.629-0.652, p = 0.012-0.016), whereas AVLTN7 improvement was negatively associated with absolute delta-power changes across Pz, P1, P2, and P5 (coefficients = -0.418 to -0.613, p = 0.020-0.048). Although these correlations did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons, they showed a relatively consistent direction across multiple electrodes. Relative and absolute delta power may reflect complementary aspects of spectral modulation. The convergent cross-electrode associations provide preliminary EEG evidence linked to cognitive response to taVNS. Parietal delta-band power may represent a candidate electrophysiological marker of cognitive change following taVNS in MCI. These exploratory findings support further validation of predefined EEG biomarkers in larger, prospectively powered studies. http://www.chictr.org.cn (ID: ChiCTR2000038868).

papers.title: Integrative analysis of Alzheimer's disease molecular networks with circadian regulators for prioritization of drug repurposing candidates.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by complex molecular mechanisms. Growing evidence indicates that circadian rhythm disruption contributes to disease progression and interacts with pathogenic pathways. Although multi-omics resources, compound perturbation profiles, and pharmacological bioactivity data are increasingly available, their integrative use for drug repurposing prioritization in AD, particularly with explicit consideration of circadian rhythm, remains limited.ObjectiveThis study aimed to prioritize drug repurposing candidates for AD, by integrating heterogeneous biological and pharmacological data.MethodsWe applied an integrative, systems-level computational analysis to prioritize drug repurposing and repositioning candidates for AD by combining network-based gene prioritization, functional transcriptomic similarity analysis, and target-level bioactivity prediction. Disease-associated molecular modules were identified within the human protein-protein interaction network, with circadian rhythm regulators incorporated as an additional disease relevant biological context. These modules were represented using functional gene embeddings to rank compound perturbation signatures. Candidate compounds were subsequently refined through ligand-based bioactivity prediction across AD associated targets to support polypharmacological prioritization.ResultsThe analysis prioritized compounds supported by convergent network-level disease relevance, transcriptomic similarity, and predicted target engagement. Several drugs previously investigated in dementia-related clinical trials were recovered. Novel repositioning candidates, including PF-562271, MGCD-265, and BMS-777607, were identified, converging on focal adhesion kinase (FAK), PI3K-AKT, and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways enriched in AD-associated genes and implicated in circadian regulation and neuroinflammation.ConclusionsThis integrative analysis identifies mechanistically coherent repurposing candidates, associated with circadian and inflammatory pathways, supporting systems-based strategies for therapeutic prioritization in complex neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Chronotherapeutic and Circadian Rhythm-Based Strategies in Diabetes Management: A Critical Opinion Based on Evidences.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is one of the world's leading health problems, and standard approaches to therapy do not take into consideration the impact of circadian misalignment on metabolic health. Chronobiological processes are involved in regulating glucose homeostasis, insulin release, hepatic glucose production, lipids, and energy metabolism; hence, disruptions such as those caused by non-rhythmic sleep patterns, shifts at work, irregular meal times, and light exposure could cause insulin resistance and even type 2 diabetes. The current critical review discusses the light-melatonin interaction and personalized chronobiological medicine. Instead of giving a descriptive account of particular treatments, the paper introduces the integrative importance of chronobiology for the management of diabetes by considering data about chrononutrition, time-restricted feeding, chronopharmacology, chrono-exercise, and an approach to chronometabolism based on the integration of the timing of meals, drugs, exercise, sleep, and light exposure with chronotype, metabolic phenotype, and the feasibility of the therapy. Circadian timing can be a promising adjuvant in the treatment of diabetes; however, the available evidence does not suggest an ideal time for intervention. Further studies should focus on measuring time, well-powered randomized controlled trials, long-term outcomes, and individualization of chronotherapy.

papers.title: A systemic circadian nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) signal engages the unfolded protein response and adipogenesis via the prefoldin complex.
papers.abstract: Daily light-dark cycles impose environmental fluctuations that require coordinated regulation of physiology. This coordination is mediated by the circadian clock, which operates as a network of tissue oscillators; however, the signals that convey circadian information between organs remain incompletely defined. We identify nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) as a circulating metabolite whose rhythmicity depends on the liver clock. In adipocytes and neuronal cells, NaR engages the unfolded protein response (UPR). Proteome-wide stability profiling implicates the prefoldin complex as a target of NaR, linking NaR exposure to altered proteostasis. In adipocytes, NaR-induced UPR signaling converges on the transcription factor CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha (CEBPA). Sustained NaR exposure suppresses adipocyte lipid deposition, whereas temporally restricted NaR stimulation enhances adipogenesis. Together, these findings identify NaR as a liver clock-controlled circulating metabolite that couples systemic circadian metabolism to proteostasis and tissue remodeling, revealing a mechanism by which temporal metabolic signals shape tissue-specific physiological outcomes.

papers.title: Night-to-night sleep variability and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a prospective cohort study with a complementary in vitro circadian-disruption experiment.
papers.abstract: Irregular sleep-wake patterns may disrupt circadian rhythms, but the dose-response relationship between night-to-night sleep variability and mortality and the association of sleep onset variability with death remain unclear. Using 4-7 valid days of wrist accelerometer data, including ≥1 weekend day, from 7,604 adults aged ≥20 years in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011-2014, linked to mortality through December 2019, we examined the within-person SDs of sleep midpoint, sleep onset, and total sleep time across nights and the sleep regularity index (SRI) in relation to all-cause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality. Survey-weighted Cox models were fitted across 20 imputed datasets and combined using Rubin's rules. Restricted cubic splines examined dose-response relationships. Complementary categorical, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were conducted. Human umbilical vein endothelial cell (HUVEC) experiments repeated in three independent runs compared cellular responses under a regular dexamethasone schedule and four prespecified irregular schedule variants. Over a median follow-up of 81 months, 714 all-cause and 229 CVD deaths occurred. Each 1-hour increase in the across-night SD of sleep midpoint, sleep onset, and total sleep time was associated with all-cause mortality HRs of 1.22 (95% CI, 1.12-1.33), 1.19 (1.11-1.29), and 1.17 (1.05-1.31), respectively. The corresponding CVD mortality HRs were 1.21 (1.09-1.35), 1.22 (1.05-1.42), and 1.16 (0.94-1.42), respectively. Each 10-point lower SRI was associated with all-cause mortality (HR, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.21-1.38) and CVD mortality (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.18-1.45). Across three independent HUVEC runs, the mean response across the four prespecified irregular schedule variants showed lower core clock-gene expression, lower Griess assay absorbance, and higher inflammatory and adhesion-marker expression than the regular schedule. Greater night-to-night sleep irregularity was associated with higher hazards of all-cause and CVD mortality, although these associations were modest compared with those of older age, hypertension, and diabetes in the same models. The complementary cellular experiment showed differences between the regular dexamethasone schedule and the prespecified irregular schedule set.

papers.title: Effects of General Anaesthesia on the Sleep Structure of Patients With Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC) and are closely correlated with clinical outcomes. With an increasing number of pDoC patients undergoing surgery under general anaesthesia (GA), this study characterized sleep patterns in pDoC patients and evaluated the effects of GA on consciousness and nocturnal sleep. We prospectively enrolled 30 pDoC patients (14 in vegetative state [VS] and 16 in minimally conscious state [MCS]) undergoing spinal cord stimulation and 12 healthy controls. Among pDoC patients, 19 (10 VS, 9 MCS) with complete pre- and postoperative PSG data were analysed for GA effects. Controls underwent one overnight polysomnography (PSG); pDoC patients underwent pre- and postoperative PSG. Consciousness was assessed with Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) before and after surgery. Compared with controls, pDoC patients presented significantly impaired sleep structure, including reduced total sleep time (TST), decreased NREM Stage 2 sleep, diminished slow-wave sleep (SWS), reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep duration and percentage relative to TST (all p < 0.05). No significant short-term changes in CRS-R scores were observed following GA. Although GA significantly prolonged TST (p = 0.039), with numerical increases in absolute NREM and SWS durations, no statistically significant changes were observed in sleep stage percentages relative to TST (all p > 0.05). Subgroup analysis showed no significant within-group changes in sleep stage percentages in either the VS or MCS group. These findings suggest that GA increases TST without statistically significant changes in sleep structure in pDoC patients.

papers.title: Chrononutrition in the aging era: Circadian regulation of metabolism, resilience, and healthy longevity.
papers.abstract: The increasing prevalence of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and age-related disorders has been linked to a growing mismatch between modern lifestyles and the biological rhythms that regulate human physiology. Chrononutrition, which explores the interaction between meal timing, circadian rhythms, and metabolism, has emerged as a promising strategy to improve metabolic health and support healthy aging. This review examines the molecular and physiological foundations of chrononutrition, focusing on the interplay between central and peripheral circadian clocks, metabolic regulation, and aging processes. We discuss the role of environmental and behavioural zeitgebers, including light exposure, feeding schedules, sleep, and physical activity, in maintaining circadian alignment and metabolic homeostasis. Attention is given to Time-Restricted Eating (TRE) and related meal-timing interventions. Current evidence indicates that aligning food intake with endogenous circadian rhythms improves insulin sensitivity, metabolic flexibility, lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation, and inflammatory balance, often independently of weight loss. Mechanistically, chrononutrition may also modulate key biological processes associated with aging, including mitochondrial function, autophagy, nutrient sensing, oxidative stress, and inflammaging. By restoring temporal organization across physiological systems, chrononutrition may enhance metabolic resilience and contribute to healthspan extension. Future studies should clarify its long-term effects on biological aging, resilience, and healthy longevity, while defining personalized interventions based on circadian phenotypes.

papers.title: Effectiveness of school-based sleep promotion programs for adolescents: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: The objective of this review is to assess the effectiveness of school-based sleep promotion programs for adolescents on sleep knowledge, sleep hygiene, sleep quality, sleep behavior, sleep efficiency, health-related quality of life, and depressive or anxiety symptoms. Adolescence is a critical period for physical and mental development, during which, quality sleep is essential. However, many adolescents experience sleep deprivation due to factors such as excessive electronic device use, academic and peer pressures, stress, and anxiety. School-based sleep promotion programs have been proposed to address these issues, but their effectiveness remains unclear. This review included studies published in English, Spanish, and Portuguese that assessed the effectiveness of school-based sleep promotion programs for adolescents aged 10 to 19 years on sleep knowledge, sleep hygiene, sleep quality, sleep efficiency, sleep behavior, health-related quality of life, and depressive or anxiety symptoms. Both randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies, with or without a comparator, were eligible. A comprehensive search strategy was used to identify relevant published and unpublished studies. Studies meeting the eligibility criteria were retrieved and their methodological quality was assessed by 2 independent reviewers using the JBI critical appraisal checklists for randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies. Quantitative data were extracted using the standardized data extraction tool. Studies were pooled for statistical meta-analysis. Effect sizes were expressed as final post-intervention standardized mean differences, and their 95% CI were calculated. Heterogeneity was assessed statistically using the standard χ2 and I2 tests. Statistical analyses were performed using random-effects models and fixed-effect models. Where statistical pooling was not possible, the findings were presented in narrative format. A total of 34 studies met the inclusion criteria, with a total of 22,679 adolescents. Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials showed statistically significant differences for sleep knowledge (SMD=0.99, 95% CI=0.48 to 1.50, P<0.001), sleep hygiene (SMD=-0.20, 95% CI=-0.31 to -0.09, P=0.0003), and depressive symptoms (SMD=-0.70, 95% CI=-1.12 to -0.29, P<0.001). No statistically significant differences were found for sleep quality (SMD=0.06, 95% CI=-0.16 to 0.27, P=0.62), sleep efficiency (SMD=0.12, 95% CI=-0.02 to 0.26, P=0.09), sleep behavior-total sleep time/sleep duration (SMD=0.69, 95% CI=-0.27 to 1.65, P=0.16), and sleep behavior-sleep onset latency (SMD=-0.88, 95% CI=-1.77 to 0.01, P=0.05). Large effect sizes were observed for sleep knowledge and sleep onset latency; moderate-to-large effects for depressive symptoms and total sleep time; and small effects for sleep hygiene, sleep efficiency, and sleep quality. The funnel plot for sleep knowledge did not suggest publication bias, and Egger's test was not statistically significant. These findings suggest that school-based sleep promotion programs can be effective in improving adolescents' sleep knowledge and sleep hygiene, and reduce depressive symptoms. However, the high variability in intervention designs and methodological quality highlights the need for further high-quality studies to identify the most effective components of these programs and clarify their long-term impacts. papers.title: Does chronic occupational demand alter EEG stress biomarkers during cognitive challenge? a study of emergency physicians.
papers.abstract: Acute cognitive challenge produces consistent changes in several EEG indices, including alpha-band desynchronization, frontocentral theta enhancement, beta-band activity, and the theta/beta ratio. These measures serve as common biomarkers of cognitive workload and stress. It is not yet clear whether chronic occupational exposure to high cognitive demand alters these responses. Emergency physicians offer a useful test case, since their work involves repeated cognitive control under time pressure and high-stakes decision-making. We recorded 19-channel electroencephalography from 17 board-certified emergency physicians and 18 non-healthcare comparison participants during eyes-open rest and a standardized composite challenge combining Stroop interference, serial subtraction, time pressure, and evaluative feedback. Spectral power was estimated with Welch's method, log-transformed, and analyzed using a hierarchical framework combining six a priori regional features with electrode-wise topographic mapping. Across groups, the challenge produced robust frontal and posterior alpha suppression and increased frontocentral theta, consistent with workload-related cortical engagement. No Group x Condition interaction survived false discovery rate correction for the regional features, and no exploratory electrode-wise interaction survived correction across the full feature set. A complementary Bayesian analysis yielded moderate evidence for the null for the alpha and theta features, but inconclusive evidence for the beta and theta/beta features. Sub-band decomposition showed the challenge-related beta increase was specific to high beta (20-30 Hz), while low and mid beta decreased in emergency physicians. These results indicate an absence of detectable large group differences in EEG stress biomarkers following prolonged occupational exposure to high cognitive demand, although the sample constrains this conclusion to large effects.

papers.title: Impact of environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing on the transcriptome of three porcine brain tissues.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment and mixing represent two management procedures in pig production with opposing effects: while environmental enrichment can promote welfare by reducing stress, repeated mixing often induces stress and can negatively impact welfare. Despite their importance in pig husbandry, how these opposing management procedures affect brain function at the molecular level remains poorly understood. This study investigated how environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing influence gene expression patterns across three porcine brain regions: hypothalamus, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. Using RNA sequencing, we analyzed brain tissues from 48 gilts subjected to a 2 × 2 factorial design comparing enrichment conditions (enriched vs. barren) and allostatic load (repeated vs. minimal mixing). While environmental enrichment showed minimal impact on gene expression, allostatic load resulted in 38 differentially expressed genes in the hippocampus, primarily involved in hormone regulation, protein transport, and neuronal activity. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) identified modules moderately correlated with experimental conditions: six modules in hippocampus associated with allostatic load, and four modules in hypothalamus associated with enrichment. Functional annotation revealed that these modules were primarily enriched in biological processes related to synaptic signaling, neuron development, and metabolic activity. Hub genes from these modules were identified, and turned out not to overlap with differentially expressed genes. Our findings suggest that based on this experimental design, the hippocampus may be particularly responsive to stress-induced transcriptomic changes, while the molecular effects of the environmental enrichment appear more subtle. Overall, this study reveals limited but region-specific transcriptional responses to allostatic load in the porcine brain.

papers.title: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation versus sham stimulation for suicidal ideation and psychiatric symptoms in depressive disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Suicidal ideation, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and sleep disturbance remain difficult to manage in psychiatric populations, and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) has emerged as an accelerated, non-invasive neuromodulation strategy for these outcomes. This meta-analysis compares iTBS versus sham-iTBS across suicidal ideation, depression severity, anxiety severity, and sleep quality to guide clinical decision-making. We systematically searched relevant electronic databases in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Continuous outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals using random-effects inverse-variance models in RevMan 5.4. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and χ 2 statistics, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Six studies were included. iTBS significantly reduced suicidal ideation versus sham-iTBS (SMD = -0.51; 95% CI: -0.93 to -0.09; p = 0.02; I 2 = 70%; n = 181 vs. 157), and the effect remained significant with lower heterogeneity after exclusion of Qin et al. (p = 0.02; I 2 = 29%). Depression severity improved with iTBS (SMD = -1.06; 95% CI: -1.64 to -0.48; p = 0.0003; I 2 = 80%; n = 162 vs. 142), with heterogeneity decreasing to 24% after exclusion of Huang et al. Anxiety severity also improved (SMD = -0.68; 95% CI: -1.27 to -0.09; p = 0.02; I 2 = 79%; n = 139 vs. 120), and heterogeneity decreased to 38% after exclusion of Huang et al. Sleep quality did not differ significantly between groups (SMD = -0.32; 95% CI: -0.98 to 0.34; p = 0.35; I 2 = 67%; n = 75 vs. 49), based on two trials. iTBS was associated with a reduction in suicidal ideation compared with sham stimulation, but the small evidence base and between-study heterogeneity limit certainty. Secondary analyses suggested improvements in depression and anxiety severity, whereas sleep quality did not differ between groups. Larger, standardized randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are needed to determine the magnitude and durability of any antisuicidal effect.

papers.title: A comprehensive investigation into EEG spectral analysis for ADHD brain dominance.
papers.abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that significantly impacts the cognitive functions and behaviour of individuals. It is characterized by abnormal brain lateralization in key brain regions linked to attention and cognitive control. This study aimed to explore and analyze the brainwave patterns linked to left and right brain dominance in ADHD, ADHD subtype, and control group using electroencephalography (EEG) spectral features, which have not been investigated in prior studies. Our study examined variations in alpha, beta, theta, and other frequency bands between the brain's left and right hemispheres, employing methodologies like EEG recordings with topographical views and statistical tests. The Asymmetric Index findings suggest a differential power spectrum density (PSD) pattern in ADHD subjects, with a higher average PSD in the right brain (RB) during working states and in the left brain (LB) during resting states. In addition, our corroborative study also uncovered that in ADHD subjects, theta and alpha waves are more dominant in the left hemispheric region, irrespective of the task state, and theta waves are notably prominent in the frontal region. The results of our novel study, supported by statistical analyses and topographical views, not only enhance our understanding of ADHD but also open avenues for more targeted and effective approaches in diagnosing and understanding the neurobiological underpinnings of ADHD and its subtypes.

papers.title: Migration Characteristics and Mechanism of Active Components From Jieyu Anshen Granule in Different Insomnia Mouse Models.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a highly prevalent disorder with substantial health and socioeconomic impacts, for which traditional Chinese medicine is an important treatment option. Jieyu Anshen Granule (JYAS-G) shows excellent clinical efficacy in insomnia treatment, but its active components, in vivo migration characteristics and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Two mouse insomnia models induced by p-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA, chemical method) and sleep deprivation machine (SDM, physical method) were established respectively, and mice were administered with low and high doses of JYAS-G, with open field test used to evaluate the pharmacodynamic effects. UHPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS combined with GNPS was applied to systematically identify the in vitro components of JYAS-G and its migration profiles in mouse plasma, liver, heart, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and hypothalamus. The SDM model induced insomnia with manic-like behaviors, which were significantly ameliorated by JYAS-G, whereas the PCPA model produced no significant insomnia-like phenotypes under the current conditions. In total, 89 in vitro components and 43 blood-absorbed components of JYAS-G were identified, showing marked tissue-specific distribution. Network pharmacology and molecular docking identified core components, including furanogermenone and curcumenol, predicted to exert anti-insomnia effects by targeting ADORA2A, GABRB3, and SLC6A4 and regulating the neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathway. This study characterizes the in vivo migration characteristics of JYAS-G and provides insights into its multi-target anti-insomnia mechanism, while comparing the modeling differences between two common insomnia animal models. These findings provide scientific evidence for the rational clinical application and further development of JYAS-G.

papers.title: Prophylactic oral diosgenin attenuates acute sleep deprivation-induced liver injury in mice via modulation of the gut microbiota and vascular barrier.
papers.abstract: Acute sleep deprivation (SD) is an increasingly prevalent health risk, yet the early inflammatory processes associated with acute hepatic injury following SD remain largely elusive. Under the rotating-platform paradigm in mice, 24-hour SD (SD24h) was associated with acute hepatic inflammation, increased overall intestinal permeability, gut vascular barrier (GVB)-associated alterations, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and elevated intestinal and hepatic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels. Fecal microbiota transplantation further showed that microbiota from SD24h donors transferred part of the hepato-intestinal inflammatory and barrier-associated phenotypes to antibiotic-pretreated recipients, whereas microbiota from DG-pretreated SD24h donors transferred an attenuated phenotype. Collectively, these findings support the involvement of the gut microbiota and intestinal barrier in acute SD-associated liver injury and indicate that prophylactic oral DG pretreatment attenuates these hepato-intestinal responses.

papers.title: Epilepsy in Children with Celiac Disease: Clinical and Electroencephalographic Characteristics and Outcomes in a Ten-Patient Case Series.
papers.abstract: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by gluten exposure in genetically predisposed individuals. Epilepsy has been reported among the neurological manifestations associated with celiac disease; however, the relationship between epilepsy and celiac disease remains incompletely understood, and their coexistence does not necessarily imply causality. This ten-patient case series describes the clinical, electroencephalographic, and follow-up characteristics of children with both epilepsy and celiac disease. Seven patients had focal epilepsy, whereas three had generalized epilepsy phenotypes, including presumed juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, presumed juvenile absence epilepsy, and sleep-related generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electroencephalography most commonly demonstrated posterior epileptiform abnormalities. Following initiation of a gluten-free diet and appropriate antiseizure medication, seizure freedom was achieved in all patients during follow-up. These findings suggest that epilepsy may occur in children with celiac disease and that favorable outcomes may be observed after dietary treatment. However, the present data should be interpreted as an association rather than evidence of causality.

papers.title: Comprehensive Multimodal Diagnostics and Rehabilitation in Persistent Post-Concussion Syndrome Following Motor Vehicle Collision.
papers.abstract: Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) are among the most common mechanisms of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), and a meaningful proportion of affected individuals develop persistent post-concussion syndrome (PPCS) characterized by prolonged multidomain dysfunction. Conventional neuroimaging frequently fails to capture the underlying pathophysiology, leaving clinicians without objective diagnostic evidence. We describe a 57-year-old woman who sustained mTBI in a rear-end MVC in March 2023. Head computed tomography (CT) performed at the emergency department and a subsequent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were both unremarkable. Despite normal structural neuroimaging, comprehensive multimodal functional assessment identified functional abnormalities across eight domains: vestibular function (videonystagmography (VNG)), cortical electrophysiology (quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG)), pupillary autonomics (automated infrared pupillometry), postural stability (computerized dynamic posturography (CDP)), oculomotor control (saccadometry), cardiac autonomic regulation (24-h heart rate variability (HRV)), olfaction (University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT)), and computerized concussion assessment (C3 Logix). Standardized psychological assessments confirmed moderate depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) = 14), moderate anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) = 12), clinically significant post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms (PTSD Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) (PCL-5 = 38)), and substantial headache impact (Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) = 58). The patient underwent a 10-modality individualized rehabilitation program. Concussion Symptom Checklist (CSC) scores declined from 92 at initial presentation to 0 by July 2023 (17 weeks post-injury), with near-complete re-resolution to 8 by February 2024 following a transient stress-related exacerbation. When conventional neuroimaging is unremarkable, comprehensive multimodal functional testing may provide evidence consistent with mTBI pathophysiology and help guide targeted rehabilitation. This case illustrates the potential value of a systematic, multimodal approach in PPCS management, while acknowledging that definitive attribution of findings to the index injury is constrained by the single-case design and absence of a pre-injury functional baseline.

papers.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for anxiety symptoms across fear, trauma, and disease contexts: a narrative review of clinical evidence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Anxiety symptoms occur in primary anxiety disorders as well as fear-, trauma-, and disease-related contexts, creating a need for safe and accessible non-pharmacological interventions. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation approach that may influence central and autonomic networks through auricular vagal pathways. This narrative review summarizes clinical evidence, stimulation parameters, safety findings, and potential mechanisms of taVNS for anxiety symptoms across these contexts. Peer-reviewed studies were identified through searches of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Scopus up to June 2026. Eligible original human studies examining taVNS in anxiety symptoms, anxiety disorders, fear-learning paradigms, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)-related symptoms, and comorbid or disease-related anxiety were synthesized narratively. Key methodological features, stimulation protocols, comparators, safety findings, and quantitative outcomes were extracted when available. Current evidence suggests that taVNS may improve selected anxiety-related symptoms, fear-extinction processes, PTSD-related hyperarousal, sleep outcomes, and autonomic nervous system parameters. Short-term studies generally report acceptable tolerability, with mostly mild adverse events. However, stimulation protocols, control designs, and outcome measures varied across studies. taVNS may be a promising adjunctive approach for anxiety symptoms across heterogeneous clinical and experimental contexts. Larger sham-controlled studies with standardised parameters and longer follow-up are needed to clarify efficacy, optimal stimulation protocols, and long-term safety.

papers.title: Sustained Seizure Freedom After Stereo-Electroencephalography Without Definitive Intervention: Evidence for Network Modulation by Invasive EEG.
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) is a diagnostic technique used to localize seizure-onset networks in drug-resistant epilepsy, typically guiding resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Sustained seizure freedom after diagnostic implantation alone is rarely described. We describe two patients who achieved long-term remission after sEEG monitoring without definitive surgical intervention. A 39-year-old man with posttraumatic right hemispheric epilepsy underwent implantation of 11 depth electrodes, during which no habitual seizures were captured despite medication withdrawal and provocation. After electrode explantation, he discontinued all antiseizure medications and has remained seizure-free for 71 months. A 63-year-old woman with left temporal epilepsy underwent implantation of 12 depth electrodes; monitoring again failed to capture habitual seizures, although abundant mesial temporal interictal discharges were recorded. After explantation, which was complicated by a small tract hemorrhage, she has remained seizure-free for 20 months on stable cenobamate therapy. These cases add to a limited body of evidence suggesting that sEEG implantation may induce microlesional or network-modulatory effects capable of interrupting seizure propagation, analogous to remission reported after intracranial electrode placement in prior series. Recognition of this phenomenon is clinically important. When no habitual seizures are recorded and early postoperative improvement is observed, a period of extended follow-up may be warranted before pursuing resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Further study is needed to define predictors of remission, clarify underlying mechanisms, and guide patient counseling regarding this uncommon but meaningful effect of invasive EEG.

papers.title: Integrative EEG/fMRI evidence for a multi-scale network underlying self-face and personal-object recognition.
papers.abstract: The sense of ownership of our faces and possessions shapes our visual perception. While the neural basis of self-face recognition has been well-studied, the neural basis of recognizing personally owned objects remains poorly understood. The main aim of this study was to investigate brain activity underlying self-face and personal object recognition, with a particular focus on the extent to which the ownership processing can be characterized as either domain-general and/or stimulus-specific. We first review the relevant literature and then report findings from two experiments - one using EEG and the other fMRI - in which the same 30 participants categorized images of faces and objects as either "mine" or "others". EEG results revealed ownership-related visuo-midfrontal activity, reflected in event-related potentials (visual P1 and N170, and midfrontal N150 and SMN), frequency-specific inter-source phase coherence (in theta band), and brain-wide time-frequency power dynamics (in alpha, beta, and theta bands). fMRI results identified ownership-related activity in four right hemisphere regions: the inferior temporal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, and superior parietal lobule; each of which formed distinct ownership-related subnetworks. The findings support "a hybrid model" in which stimulus-specific visual pathways (e.g., face-sensitive regions) interact with domain-general frontal activity encoding self-relevance. This integrative evidence clarifies how a dynamic, multi-scale network underlying ownership perception is constructed across time, frequency, and brain space.

papers.title: Circadian melatonin suppression and vitamin D deficiency disrupt aortic reactivity via MT1/MT2 and VDR-dependent mechanisms in rats.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and vitamin D deficiency (VDD) are increasingly prevalent and independently associated with cardiovascular dysfunction. However, their combined impact on vascular reactivity and receptor signaling remains insufficiently defined. This study investigated the independent and interactive effects of melatonin (MEL) suppression induced by continuous light (CL) or pinealectomy (Px) and VDD on vascular contractility, endothelial function, and MT1/vitamin D receptor (VDR) gene expression in rat thoracic aorta. Isolated aortic rings were subjected to cumulative concentration response curves for phenylephrine (PE) and acetylcholine (ACh). Pharmacodynamic parameters, potency (pD₂), maximal efficacy (Emax), and area under the curve (AUC) were calculated. MEL and calcitriol modulation with receptor antagonism was performed to determine receptor dependence. Relative MT1 and VDR mRNA expression was quantified using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). CL, Px, and VDD significantly enhanced PE-induced maximal contraction, with the combined deficiency groups exhibiting the greatest augmentation of α₁-adrenergic responsiveness. In contrast, ACh-induced relaxation was selectively impaired under dual-deficiency conditions, characterized by reduced Emax without major changes in pD2, indicating compromised endothelial efficacy rather than altered receptor sensitivity. MEL attenuated vasoconstriction and enhanced relaxation in a receptor-dependent manner, whereas calcitriol potentiated contractility through VDR signaling. Notably, combined CL + VDD produced marked upregulation of MT1 (~ 10-fold) and VDR (~ 108-fold), suggesting compensatory transcriptional remodeling. Circadian disruption and VDD synergistically promote vascular hyperreactivity and endothelial dysfunction. Their convergence amplifies α₁-adrenergic signaling while impairing nitric oxide (NO) mediated relaxation, identifying a mechanistic axis linking modern light exposure and hypovitaminosis D to heightened cardiovascular risk.

papers.title: EEG-Derived Pain Threshold Index-Guided Remifentanil Titration During Laparoscopic Abdominal Surgery: A Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: To determine whether remifentanil titration guided by the pain threshold index (PTi), an electroencephalography-derived proxy for nociceptive tolerance rather than subjective pain, reduces intraoperative remifentanil infusion during laparoscopic abdominal surgery. In this prospective, single-center, assessor-blinded randomized trial, adults undergoing elective laparoscopic abdominal surgery with propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion were assigned 1:1 to PTi-guided or conventional hemodynamic-guided remifentanil titration. The primary endpoint was intraoperative remifentanil infusion rate. The principal analysis used the full-analysis set and covariate-adjusted linear regression with heteroskedasticity-consistent robust standard errors. Among 200 randomized patients, 195 were analyzed (98 PTi-guided; 97 control). The primary endpoint was neutral: mean (SD) remifentanil infusion rate was 7.44 (1.43) versus 7.63 (1.41) µg kg-1 h-1; adjusted mean difference, -0.06 µg kg-1 h-1 (95% CI, -0.44 to 0.32; P=0.758). Per-protocol results were similar. Median (IQR) NRS at post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) admission was 2.0 (2.0-3.0) versus 3.0 (2.0-4.0), and Ramsay score was 2.0 (2.0-2.0) in both groups. In exploratory secondary analyses, rescue opioid was used in the PACU by 18/98 (18.4%) versus 31/97 (32.0%) patients and any rescue opioid through 48 h by 29/98 (29.6%) versus 44/97 (45.4%). Any postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) through 48 h occurred in 17/98 (17.3%) versus 29/97 (29.9%) patients. Total postoperative opioid exposure through 48 h was not reduced. PTi-guided remifentanil titration did not reduce intraoperative remifentanil infusion. PACU pain and sedation scores were not materially different. Lower early rescue-opioid use and fewer PONV events through 48 h were exploratory secondary findings, were not accompanied by lower postoperative opioid dose, and require prospective confirmation.

papers.title: The Neural Symphony in the Periodontium: Health, Inflammation, and Regeneration.
papers.abstract: Periodontal nerves, comprising sensory, sympathetic, and parasympathetic fibers, are essential components of the periodontium. Beyond their classic sensory and proprioceptive functions, these neural networks actively modulate periodontal immune responses, bone remodeling, and tissue regeneration. They orchestrate tissue homeostasis by releasing specific neuropeptides, neurotransmitters, and neurotrophic factors. The progression of periodontitis is intimately linked to neural dysregulation, where proinflammatory mediators (e.g., excessive substance P and sympathetic catecholamines) overpower protective signals (e.g., calcitonin gene-related peptide and parasympathetic acetylcholine). Conversely, successful periodontal regeneration requires the restoration of this neural equilibrium. Nerve terminals rapidly sprout into osteogenic zones during early repair. Subsequently, their spatiotemporally patterned signaling suppresses osteoclastogenesis and promotes the osteogenic differentiation of stem cells. Crucially, these local neural networks function as a bidirectional conduit linking the periodontium to the central nervous system: systemic stressors (eg, sleep deprivation and chronic stress) can compromise ganglionic autophagy or trigeminal function to exacerbate periodontal bone loss, while periodontal pathogens can reciprocally exploit these pathways to induce central neuroinflammation. Recognizing this interconnected oral-neural-brain axis not only explains why certain periodontitis-susceptible patients remain refractory to conventional therapies but also highlights the broader impact of periodontal inflammation on neurodegenerative risk. Furthermore, nerve-targeted strategies, including neurotrophin-functionalized biomaterials, local neuropeptide delivery, and bioelectric neuromodulation, offer promising approaches to resolving refractory inflammation, restoring periodontal integrity, and concurrently mitigating the risk of associated central neuroinflammation. In this review, we comprehensively characterize the spatiotemporal plasticity of periodontal nerves under physiological and pathological conditions. We dissect the molecular mechanisms linking neural signaling to periodontal immunity and repair, and highlight how integrating neurobiology into periodontology could advance the development of next-generation regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Acute Onset Orolingual Choreoathetosis and Auditory Hallucinations in a Healthy Young Adult Following High Melatonin Dose.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is considered a safe OTC sleep aid with rarely reported adverse effects despite limited data. We present a case of acute orolingual choreoathetosis and auditory hallucinations following 132 mg ingestion of melatonin in an otherwise healthy, 22-year-old active-duty male in IBOLC training. The patient developed abrupt, predominantly orolingual choreoathetosis and mild auditory hallucinations, 1 hour after waking. Three days earlier, he began taking 24 mg of melatonin nightly for insomnia and ingested 132 mg the night before presentation. He denied alcohol, illicit drug, or other medication use. On ED arrival, he was hemodynamically stable with continuous orolingual choreoathetosis. Initial labs demonstrated mild acute kidney injury and transaminitis. Head CT was unremarkable. MRI head showed a nonspecific left frontal white matter hyperintensity. Lumbar puncture revealed normal protein and WBC, negative culture, and negative oligoclonal bands, though CSF processing difficulties prevented autoimmune panel completion. Neurologic symptoms resolved by the next morning without recurrence, and a subsequent EEG was unremarkable. This case documents a temporal association between high-dose melatonin exposure and acute neurologic symptoms but does not establish melatonin as the cause. The clinical presentation also occurred in the setting of substantial confounders, including sleep deprivation and heat exposure. This observation supports further investigation of uncommon neurologic presentations occurring after high-dose melatonin intake.

papers.title: Possible Epstein-Barr virus-associated central nervous system involvement with reversible electroencephalographic abnormalities in a child: a case report.
papers.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated central nervous system (CNS) involvement in children is uncommon and may present with nonspecific neurological symptoms. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may remain normal, making diagnosis challenging. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) has emerged as a useful diagnostic tool, although positive EBV results require careful clinical interpretation. A previously healthy 5-year-old boy presented with fever (38.5 ℃), headache, dizziness, and nausea for 3 days without seizures, altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, or ataxia. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers. Brain MRI was unremarkable. CSF examination revealed an opening pressure of 120 mmH2O and mild pleocytosis (13×106/L, 100% mononuclear cells), with normal glucose and protein levels. CSF tNGS detected EBV (24,002 sequence reads; estimated pathogen concentration <103 copies/mL), while no other pathogens were identified and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies were negative. Serum EBV DNA was positive, and EBV serology demonstrated viral capsid antigen (VCA)-IgM positivity during the acute phase followed by VCA-IgG seroconversion during recovery. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed sharp and sharp-slow wave discharges in the left parietal, occipital, and posterior temporal regions despite normal MRI. The patient received intravenous ganciclovir (10 mg/kg twice daily for 2 weeks) and empirical ceftriaxone for 4 days. Clinical symptoms resolved completely, follow-up EEG normalized, and no neurological sequelae were observed at 1-month follow-up. This case highlights that possible EBV-associated CNS involvement may occur in children despite normal brain MRI and only mild CSF abnormalities. The combination of CSF tNGS, dynamic EBV serology, EEG findings, exclusion of alternative etiologies, and clinical follow-up may facilitate diagnosis. Because EBV detected in CSF does not necessarily indicate causation, results should always be interpreted in the context of the overall clinical presentation.

papers.title: Dual-pathway processing of AI-generated Chinese ink painting: evidence from eye-tracking, EEG, and artistic expertise.
papers.abstract: AI-driven generative art is changing the scope of artistic creation, but the principles behind its aesthetics and the perception of its outcomes remain relatively unexplored, especially concerning culturally specific art forms. The present study investigates how viewers cognitively, affectively, and evaluatively process AI-generated Chinese ink paintings, and whether artistic expertise moderates these responses. We introduce the concept of expressive expansion as a viewer-perceived psychological effect - the tendency for AI-generated ink works to elicit higher ratings of expressiveness and dynamic tension than traditional counterparts - and examine its neural and behavioral correlates using a multimodal paradigm. Stimuli generated using a pre-trained Stable Diffusion architecture were assessed according to three aesthetic metrics along with traditional and digital non-AI artworks by 120 respondents equally split into professional artists and non-artists. Multidimensional measurement based on eye-tracking, semantic differential rating, and EEG showed that, under blind viewing conditions, AI-generated stimuli yielded significantly greater scan-path entropy and beta band suppression than traditional and digital non-AI works, suggesting that they engaged broader attentional exploration and increased attentional engagement as indexed by implicit behavioral and neural measures. Professional and non-professional evaluators agreed on expressiveness evaluation scores but differed considerably in their cultural authenticity perception, suggesting a dissociation between aesthetic appeal and cultural validity. These findings are consistent with a dual-pathway interpretive framework in which perceptual-affective and cultural-evaluative responses can dissociate as a function of artistic expertise - an account advanced as consistent with the observed dissociation rather than as a mechanism established by the present data - and contribute to the emerging empirical literature on audience responses to AI-generated art in culturally specific domains. All conclusions are restricted to the selected stimulus sets under the present experimental conditions. The source code, LoRA model weights, and experimental datasets will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/15100376058/ink-painting-ai-expressive-expansion (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20540420).
